newsitem.title: CHINA: Asian Gold-Rally seen shortlived, demand holding.
newsitem.headline: Asian Gold-Rally seen shortlived, demand holding.

text.p: Signs of a rally in bullion prices sparked excitement among Asian gold dealers on Friday, but some warned that an upswing was unlikely to be sustained.
A sharp slide in the U.S. dollar was providing impetus to push gold out of its recent $339-344 an ounce range, a dealer with a Western bank said.
London gold ended $3.05 higher at $343.65/344.15 after New York-led fund buying, which Asian gold dealers said was a reaction to the weaker U.S. dollar and confusing signals from equities markets.
Comments on Thursday by Japanese Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara that the yen could strengthen to 103 to the dollar triggered a sell-off in the U.S. currency.
At 0300 GMT on Friday, the dollar stood at 122.65 yen, down from 123.67 yen at the close of New York trading.
The fiasco at Canada's Bre-X Minerals Ltd would not have a large long-term impact on gold values, an analyst said.
Bre-X revealed last weekend that a deposit in Indonesia it had touted as the century's richest gold strike was in fact worthless.
"People will have factored that in, and it will just be a background factor," the analyst said. "As there is no gold there, that's 70 million ounces less for the market."
He put the current rally in gold down to rumours of central bank selling earlier in the week which had failed to push prices down.
"People see that if this news had been absorbed without pushing prices down, then it is good for the market," he said.
"But it's bad news," he added, because central bank selling, if it happened, would be taking up slack in the market that would otherwise have been available to producers later in the year.
One Hong Kong dealer saw stiff resistance at $345 an ounce for the remainder of 1997.
"I think we are stuck," he said. "I think we are trading $335-345 for 1997 and any movement out of that range will be a short-lived spike either way -- though $330 will have a lot of support."
Another dealing source in Hong Kong said physical demand in the region was healthy enough to keep Hong Kong premiums at US$1.00 above London -- down from a peak in February of $1.50.
Any sustained rally, however, would see demand and premiums start to soften, he said.
In Southeast Asia, buyers from Indonesia have shied away from the market.
"I sense demand from Indonesia is slowing down because of fluctuations in the rupiah," a trader in Singapore said, adding the sluggish Thai economy has also knocked sales lower.
"There's also not much interest from people like the Australian producers. There's really not much interest around for gold these days," a bank dealer in the island state said.
Singapore premiums over spot London prices had sagged due to a slowdown in demand, traders said.
They were quoted slightly easier at 80-100 U.S. cents an ounce compared with last week's 85-110 cents.
-- Lynne O'Donnell, Shanghai newsroom (86-21) 6279-8544
-- Rene Pastor, Singapore Newsroom (65) 870-3305)
